newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bosnia-bound U.S. troops not mission creep-colonel.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia-bound U.S. troops not mission creep-colonel.

text.p: The U.S. military commander who will lead a new wave of soldiers into Bosnia said on Friday he saw no sign of "mission creep" in the 30 percent rise in U.S. troops planned for the troubled Balkans.

"My mission is very specific and right now I have no indication of mission creep," said U.S. army Colonel Michael Thompson, the commanding officer of the First Infantry Division's Second Brigade based in Schweinfurt.

"We are very cognisant of mission creep and we are dedicated to making sure we understand our mission. From an operational basis our force is adequate and proper for this mission," Thompson told Reuters in an interview.

Some 5,000 U.S. troops from Germany will begin moving into Bosnia within days to help cover the withdrawal of about 52,000 international peacekeepers, including 15,000 U.S. soldiers, in a mission expected to last at least until March.

But the NATO peacekeeping force formally ends its mission on December 20 and news that the mission will not be over until March had sparked claims that U.S. President Bill Clinton misled his country about troops in Bosnia.

The U.S. Congress sharply criticised U.S. Secretary of Defense William Perry on Thursday after he left open the possibility that U.S. forces could be part of a potential new NATO-led follow-on peacekeeping force in 1997.
Thompson declined to predict when his troops would leave Bosnia, saying his mission orders were only until December 20, when the year-long U.N. mission mandate ends.
"I cannot speculate on political decisions," he said. "It serves no purpose. My mission right now is until December 20 and we are going to fulfil those orders."
The December pullout date has already slipped weeks into early 1997, because a NATO-led force is being kept longer to help keep peace during municipal elections in November.
Republicans have demanded that Congress have a final say on whether U.S. forces are again committed to Bosnia as part of a follow-on force in which allies want to see U.S. participation.
The new U.S. troops have been dubbed a "covering force" to help in particular with the pullout of the army's First Armoured division, when given approval to leave Bosnia.

On Friday soldiers set to join the Implementation Force (IFOR) packed gear and prepared equipment that will be loaded onto trains next week and shipped to a staging ground in Hungary before the road journey through Croatia into Bosnia.
Thompson said the deployment would be easier than that faced by the initial U.S. forces sent from Germany last December and that his command saw a priority in fighting complacency.

"It is a threat. Complacency cannot be a danger for our troops. We guard against complacency by training. If the days become routine, then we implement training and we will do training exercises in Bosnia to sharpen our skills," he said.

Sergeant Warren Warr of Biloxi, Mississippi, a gunner on a Bradley armoured fighting vehicle, said soldiers were relieved that the orders had come through after months of training. "We are ready to go. We are ready to roll," he said.
Ian Maxwell of Reedsport, Oregon, said he was excited about the mission. "But it will be pretty rough. My wife is having a baby in March and hopefully we will be back in time."
But his wife, pregnant with their first child, was upset about the mission. "I just don't understand why more soldiers have to go," she said, declining to give her first name.
